graph_adjacency__vertex_order.definition: If A uses order v₁,…,vₙ and A′ uses vₚ₁,…,vₚₙ, then A′ᵢⱼ=Aₚᵢₚⱼ. This simultaneously applies the same vertex permutation to rows and columns.
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.explanation: A row and column jointly belong to one vertex. Permuting rows alone makes row and column orders inconsistent. Isomorphism of undirected simple graphs can be expressed as equality of adjacency matrices after a vertex reordering.
notation: A′ᵢⱼ=Aₚᵢₚⱼ.
Two graphs are isomorphic exactly when simultaneous row and column reordering by one vertex permutation makes their adjacency matrices agree.
graph_adjacency__vertex_order.example: Reordering a—b—c as (b,a,c) moves the degree-2 middle vertex’s row and column to the first position.
common_mistakes: Swapping rows without swapping columns.
Declaring graphs nonisomorphic because their matrices differ entry by entry.

graph_matrix.title: Matrix representations of graphs
graph_matrix.summary: Adjacency, incidence, and Laplacian matrices encode different aspects of a graph; distinguish their row and column objects and sign conventions.
graph_matrix.definition: Fix vertex and edge orders for an undirected simple graph. The unsigned incidence matrix M has vertices as rows and edges as columns, with entry 1 when the vertex is an endpoint, otherwise 0. After arbitrarily orienting every edge, the oriented incidence matrix B records −1 at the tail and +1 at the head. With adjacency matrix A and degree diagonal matrix D, the Laplacian is L=D−A and BBᵀ=L.
graph_matrix.explanation: Every column of M has two ones, and row sums give degrees. Every column of B has one −1 and one +1 and sums to 0. Reversing an edge’s chosen orientation negates that column without changing BBᵀ. For a loopless directed graph, Boolean unions of powers of A give reachability matrices; specify whether length-0 walks count. Reflexive reachability has ones on the diagonal. Matrix representations convert combinatorial properties into computable algebraic relations.
notation: M is the unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrix; B uses tail −1 and head +1.
D=diag(deg(v₁),…,deg(vₙ)); L=D−A=BBᵀ.
xᵀLx=Σuv∈E(xᵤ−xᵥ)² for undirected simple graphs.
graph_matrix.example: For a single edge a—b oriented a→b, B=[[-1],[1]], so BBᵀ=[[1,-1],[-1,1]], also the degree matrix I minus adjacency matrix [[0,1],[1,0]].
common_mistakes: Confusing vertex–edge incidence matrices with vertex–vertex adjacency matrices.
Mixing unsigned M with signed B and incorrectly writing MMᵀ=D−A.
Claiming reachability diagonals must all be 0 or all be 1 without stating whether length 0 is allowed.

graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.title: Unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrices
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.summary: An unsigned incidence matrix records endpoint membership, with two ones per simple undirected edge.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.definition: Fix vertex and edge orders for an undirected simple graph. In M, rows represent vertices and columns edges; an entry is 1 if the vertex is an endpoint, otherwise 0. With n vertices and m edges, M is n×m.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.explanation: Every column has exactly two ones and row sums equal degrees. MMᵀ has degrees on its diagonal and common incident-edge counts off diagonal, so MMᵀ=D+A for simple graphs.
notation: M is an n×m 0/1 matrix.
For an undirected simple graph, MMᵀ=D+A.
graph_matrix__unsigned_incidence.example: For a—b—c with edges ordered ab,bc, M=[[1,0],[1,1],[0,1]].
common_mistakes: Treating the product for unsigned M as D−A.
Reversing the row and column roles of vertices and edges without stating it.

graph_matrix__laplacian.title: Laplacian matrices and edge energy
graph_matrix__laplacian.summary: The Laplacian combines adjacency and degrees, using squared differences to reflect connectivity.
graph_matrix__laplacian.definition: For an undirected simple graph, L=D−A, where D is the degree diagonal matrix. If B uses tail −1 and head +1 in every column, then L=BBᵀ.
graph_matrix__laplacian.explanation: The diagonal of L records degrees, adjacent off-diagonal positions are −1, other entries are 0, and each row sums to 0. The quadratic form xᵀLx sums squared endpoint-value differences over edges. In a connected graph it vanishes exactly when all vertex values are equal.
notation: L=D−A=BBᵀ.
xᵀLx=Σuv∈E(xᵤ−xᵥ)².
graph_matrix__laplacian.example: For a—b—c, L=[[1,-1,0],[-1,2,-1],[0,-1,1]], with diagonal entry 2 at the middle vertex.
common_mistakes: Writing +1 in adjacent off-diagonal entries of L.
Mistaking the unsigned incidence-matrix product for D−A as well.

graph_matrix__reachability.title: Reachability matrices and Boolean operations
graph_matrix__reachability.summary: Reachability matrices record only whether a path exists; Boolean addition and multiplication reduce counts to truth values.
graph_matrix__reachability.definition: For a directed graph, the reachability matrix R has rᵢⱼ=1 if a walk of length at least 1 exists from vᵢ to vⱼ. Allowing length 0 gives the reflexive reachability matrix R*=I∨R. Boolean matrix multiplication replaces addition by OR and multiplication by AND.
graph_matrix__reachability.explanation: Ordinary Aᵏ counts walks; Boolean Aᵏ only tests existence of a length-k walk. In a finite graph, reflexive reachability is the Boolean union of I,A,…,Aⁿ⁻¹. Diagonal entries of nonreflexive R additionally require considering nonempty closed walks.
notation: (A⊙B)ᵢⱼ=∨k(aᵢk∧bkⱼ).
R*=I∨A∨A²∨…∨Aⁿ⁻¹, with Boolean powers and unions.
graph_matrix__reachability.example: In the directed diamond s→a,s→b,a→t,b→t, ordinary (A²)ₛₜ=2, while the same entry in the Boolean square is 1.
common_mistakes: Writing the count 2 into a reachability matrix restricted to 0/1.
Unconditionally omitting or imposing reflexive diagonal entries.

graph_matrix__signed_incidence.title: Oriented incidence matrices and sign conventions
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.summary: After orienting edges, each incidence column has one negative and one positive entry and sums to 0.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.definition: For a finite loopless directed graph with n≥1 vertices, fix vertex and arc orders. Its oriented incidence matrix B records −1 at the tail and +1 at the head of each arc, with zeros elsewhere. An undirected simple graph may also be arbitrarily oriented to construct B; this algebraic representation does not change its undirected traversal rules.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.explanation: Reversing an arc or a chosen edge orientation negates its column, leaving BBᵀ unchanged. Since each column sums to 0, all row vectors sum to zero, and rank is at most n−1 for n≥1. The equality BBᵀ=D−A uses B obtained by orienting an undirected simple graph and D,A from that original undirected graph. Its D,A cannot be replaced directly by a directed outdegree matrix and directed adjacency matrix.
notation: For a loopless graph, each column has exactly one −1 and one +1, and 1ᵀB=0.
For B from an arbitrary orientation of an undirected simple graph, BBᵀ=D−A, where D,A both come from that original undirected graph.
graph_matrix__signed_incidence.example: The column for a→b is [-1,1]ᵀ; reversing it gives [1,-1]ᵀ.
common_mistakes: Mixing the tail −1, head +1 convention with another convention.
Interpreting an artificial orientation as making an originally undirected edge one-way.

graph_connectivity.title: Paths and connectivity
graph_connectivity.summary: Paths express reachability; connected components divide an undirected graph into maximal internally reachable parts with no reachability between them.
graph_connectivity.definition: A walk is a sequence of adjacent vertices joined successively by edges, with length equal to edges traversed. Here a path specifically means a simple path, with no repeated vertices. An undirected graph is connected if every two vertices have a path between them. A connected component is a maximal connected subgraph, including an isolated vertex by itself. A directed graph is strongly connected if every pair is mutually reachable, and weakly connected if ignoring directions gives a connected graph.
graph_connectivity.explanation: “Maximal” means it cannot be extended by adding other vertices of the graph while staying in the same connected part, rather than having the largest vertex count. Undirected reachability uniquely partitions vertices into components. Breadth-first search visits layers and finds minimum edge-count distances from a source in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search also finds components, but its first path need not be shortest. Strong connectivity must respect arc directions; weak connectivity alone guarantees neither one-way nor mutual reachability.
notation: u⇝v means a directed path from u to v, or reachability in an undirected context.
c(G) is the number of connected components of an undirected graph.
d(u,v) is the minimum path edge count in an unweighted graph; use ∞ if unreachable.
graph_connectivity.example: The graph with vertices {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edges {ab,bc,de} has three components with vertex sets {a,b,c},{d,e},{f}. Although a and c are not adjacent, b connects them.
common_mistakes: Confusing nonadjacency with unreachability.
Omitting isolated vertices or calling every connected subgraph a component.
Ignoring directed arcs and mistaking weak for strong connectivity.

graph_connectivity__simple_paths.title: Simple paths and reachability
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.summary: Simple paths have no repeated vertices; deleting repeated portions turns any reaching walk into a simple path.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.definition: A path here means a simple path: consecutive vertices are joined by edges and all vertices are distinct; its length counts edges. A directed simple path must also follow every arc direction.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.explanation: If a walk repeats a vertex, remove the closed segment between two occurrences without changing its endpoints. Repeated deletion produces a simple path. Thus reachability does not require repeated traversal, though counting and negative-weight optimization require separate distinctions.
notation: A simple path with r edges has r+1 distinct vertices.
u⇝v denotes a path from u to v.
graph_connectivity__simple_paths.example: a—b—c—d is a simple path of length 3; a—b—a—c is not, since a repeats.
common_mistakes: Counting vertices instead of edges as path length.
Ignoring that directed paths must follow arrows.

graph_connectivity__components.title: Undirected reachability and connected components
graph_connectivity__components.summary: Undirected reachability uniquely partitions vertices into maximal connected parts.
graph_connectivity__components.definition: Vertices u,v of an undirected graph are reachable if a path connects them. Reachability is an equivalence relation; each equivalence class with all its internal edges forms a connected component. An isolated vertex is a component by itself.
graph_connectivity__components.explanation: There are no edges between different components, since such an edge would make them mutually reachable. Adding an edge between two components merges them and reduces the component count by 1. Adding an edge within one component does not change the count.
notation: c(G) is the number of connected components.
A component is a maximal connected subgraph; it need not be a largest component.
graph_connectivity__components.example: Edges {ab,cd} and isolated vertex e give 3 components. Adding bc leaves 2 components, with e still separate.
common_mistakes: Counting only parts containing edges as components.
Assuming one edge connecting two components connects all components.

graph_connectivity__strong_components.title: Strong connectivity and strongly connected components
graph_connectivity__strong_components.summary: Strong connectivity requires mutual reachability; strong components are maximal mutually reachable parts.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.definition: A directed graph is strongly connected if every pair u,v has directed paths both from u to v and from v to u. A strongly connected component is a maximal strongly connected subgraph. One vertex may form a strong component.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.explanation: An arc going only from one side to another cannot merge those sides into a single strong component. Mutual reachability partitions vertices into disjoint strong components; degrees or drawing distances do not determine this grouping.
notation: u,v share a strong component exactly when u⇝v and v⇝u.
Length 0 permits each vertex to reach itself.
graph_connectivity__strong_components.example: If a↔b and b→c, the strong components are {a,b} and {c}; c cannot return to a or b.
common_mistakes: Treating one-way reachability as sufficient for a common strong component.
Forgetting that a single vertex without a cycle can still be a strong component.

graph_connectivity__walks.title: Walks and repeated traversal
graph_connectivity__walks.summary: A walk requires an edge at every step and may repeat vertices and edges.
graph_connectivity__walks.definition: A walk is a finite alternating sequence of vertices and connecting edges, allowing repeated vertices and edges. It is closed if its starting and ending vertices coincide. A length-0 stay at one vertex may also be a walk.
graph_connectivity__walks.explanation: Adjacency-matrix powers count walks rather than only simple paths. Traversing an undirected edge and returning is legal, but both traversals use the same edge. In negative-weight problems, allowing repetition can determine whether a minimum cost exists.
notation: Length counts edge traversals, including repetitions.
A closed walk has equal endpoints and may repeat internally.
graph_connectivity__walks.example: With only edge ab, a—b—a is a closed walk of length 2 despite having only two distinct vertices and one distinct edge.
common_mistakes: Assuming walks must have distinct edges.
Excluding repeated traversals from the length count.

graph_connectivity__trails.title: Trails and the no-repeated-edge restriction
graph_connectivity__trails.summary: Trails do not repeat edges but may repeat vertices.
graph_connectivity__trails.definition: A trail is a walk with no repeated edges. A closed trail has equal endpoints and still uses each edge at most once. In a directed graph repetition is judged by arc identity; traversing an undirected edge backward repeats the same edge.
graph_connectivity__trails.explanation: Every simple path is a trail, but a trail need not be a simple path. An Euler trail covers all edges and may therefore revisit vertices where parts meet.
notation: Trail: all traversed edges are distinct.
Simple path ⇒ trail ⇒ walk; the reverse implications generally fail.
graph_connectivity__trails.example: For two triangles sharing vertex c, c—a—b—c—d—e—c is a closed trail: c repeats but no edge does.
common_mistakes: Rejecting a trail because a vertex repeats.
Failing to label parallel edges and mistaking two distinct ones for one repeated edge.

graph_connectivity__cycles.title: Simple cycles versus closed walks
graph_connectivity__cycles.summary: A simple cycle repeats no vertex except its common start and end, imposing stronger restrictions than a general closed walk.
graph_connectivity__cycles.definition: In an undirected simple graph, a simple cycle is a closed trail of length at least 3 whose vertices are distinct except for its endpoints. A directed simple cycle must follow arc directions and have distinct vertices apart from the endpoints. If loops or opposite arcs are allowed, specify minimum-length conventions separately.
graph_connectivity__cycles.explanation: Cycles supply alternative routes between vertices and underlie bridges, two-colorability, Hamiltonicity, and other concepts. A closed walk can traverse an edge back and forth or join several cycles, so it need not itself be a simple cycle.
notation: An undirected simple cycle Cₖ requires k≥3.
Repeating the initial vertex at the end only denotes closure.
graph_connectivity__cycles.example: The triangle a—b—c—a is a simple cycle. Although a—b—a is closed, it repeats one edge and is not a simple cycle in an undirected simple graph.
common_mistakes: Calling every closed walk a simple cycle.
Counting the repeated start at the end as an extra new vertex.

graph_connectivity__connected_graph.title: Connected graphs and maximal connected subgraphs
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.summary: Connectivity requires reachability between every two vertices, without requiring direct adjacency or unique paths.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.definition: An undirected graph with at least one vertex is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices. A connected subgraph requires only internal reachability; a connected component must additionally admit no extension within the original graph to a larger connected part.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.explanation: Connected does not mean complete: many pairs may connect through intermediate vertices. It does not mean a tree either, since cycles are allowed. A path connecting two vertices need not be shortest.
notation: A connected graph has c(G)=1.
Maximal means unable to be extended, rather than largest among all subgraphs.
graph_connectivity__connected_graph.example: The path a—b—c is connected although a,c are not adjacent. Edge ab alone is a connected subgraph, but is not a component of the entire graph.
common_mistakes: Equating connected with pairwise direct adjacency.
Treating every connected subgraph as a connected component.

graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.title: Weak connectivity and the underlying undirected graph
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.summary: Weak connectivity checks connections after ignoring arrows and does not guarantee actual directed reachability.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.definition: The underlying undirected graph of a directed graph is obtained by ignoring every arc direction. The directed graph is weakly connected if this underlying graph is connected; its undirected components correspond to weak components.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.explanation: Strong connectivity implies weak connectivity, but generally not conversely. Weak connectivity identifies whether a structure is separated, but does not directly determine whether directed transport or dependency routes are feasible.
notation: Strongly connected ⇒ weakly connected.
Reversing every arc leaves the underlying undirected graph unchanged.
graph_connectivity__weak_connectivity.example: With only a→b,b→c, the underlying graph is a—b—c. It is weakly connected, but c cannot reach a.
common_mistakes: Treating a route found after ignoring directions as a legal directed route.
Assuming weak and strong connectivity differ only in wording.

graph_connectivity__condensation.title: Condensation of strongly connected components
graph_connectivity__condensation.summary: Contracting strong components to vertices separates internal cycles from one-way dependencies between components.
graph_connectivity__condensation.definition: The condensation of a directed graph has its strong components as vertices. An arc between two different components exists whenever the original graph has an arc from the first to the second. Internal arcs are omitted.
graph_connectivity__condensation.explanation: The condensation is a directed acyclic graph: a cycle between components would make their union mutually reachable, contradicting maximality. It can analyze precedence between strong components.
notation: Condensation vertices are strong components, not individual original vertices.
Internal loops of components are not retained.
common_mistakes: Using weak components as condensation vertices.
Retaining internal cycles and incorrectly claiming condensations may have cycles.

graph_cut.title: Cut vertices and bridges
graph_cut.summary: Cut vertices and bridges identify vertices and edges essential to connectivity.
graph_cut.definition: In a finite undirected graph G, a vertex v is a cut vertex if deleting v and all its incident edges increases the component count. An edge e is a cut edge or bridge if deleting e while retaining all vertices increases that count. In an undirected simple graph, an edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut.explanation: Compare component counts before and after deletion; degrees alone do not decide. Internal vertices of paths are usually cut vertices, while cycle edges have alternative routes and are not bridges. Two cycles sharing one vertex may have a cut vertex with no bridge. For a connected graph on at least two vertices, edge connectivity λ(G) is the minimum number of edges whose deletion disconnects it, measuring resistance to edge failures beyond single bridges.
notation: G−v deletes v and its incident edges; G−e deletes only e.
Cut vertex: c(G−v)>c(G); bridge: c(G−e)>c(G).
λ(G) is the edge connectivity of a connected graph.
graph_cut.example: If triangles abc and def are joined only by cd, then cd is the unique bridge and c,d are cut vertices. Any triangle edge can be bypassed using its other two edges.
common_mistakes: Confusing deleting an edge with deleting its two endpoints.
Assuming a high-degree vertex must be a cut vertex, or no bridges means no cut vertices.
For a disconnected graph, asking only whether deletion leaves it disconnected rather than comparing component counts.

graph_cut__articulation.title: Cut vertices and vertex deletion
graph_cut__articulation.summary: Cut vertices are defined by an increase in component count after vertex deletion, not directly by degree.
graph_cut__articulation.definition: A vertex v is a cut vertex if deleting it and all incident edges increases the original component count. This also applies to disconnected graphs and affects only the original component containing v.
graph_cut__articulation.explanation: Removing a leaf does not break routes among the other vertices. Removing a vertex from a cycle leaves a path. A shared connection vertex of several cycles may be a cut vertex even if none of its incident edges is a bridge.
notation: v is a cut vertex exactly when c(G−v)>c(G).
Vertex deletion also deletes all incident edges.
graph_cut__articulation.example: The cut vertices of a—b—c—d are b,c; endpoints a,d are not cut vertices.
common_mistakes: Replacing increased component count with merely remaining disconnected.
Assuming every vertex of degree at least 2 is a cut vertex.

graph_cut__bridges.title: Bridges and alternative routes
graph_cut__bridges.summary: An edge is a bridge exactly when its endpoints have no alternative route after it is deleted.
graph_cut__bridges.definition: A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the component count of an undirected graph. In an undirected simple graph, uv is a bridge exactly when u,v are unreachable in G−uv, equivalently when uv lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut__bridges.explanation: Deleting one cycle edge leaves its endpoints connected by the rest, so it is not a bridge. Every tree edge has no alternative route, so every tree edge is a bridge. The graph as a whole need not be connected to test for bridges.
notation: For a bridge e, c(G−e)=c(G)+1.
A bridge lies on no simple cycle.
graph_cut__bridges.example: In triangle abc with added edge cd, cd is a bridge and the three triangle edges are not.
common_mistakes: Equating no bridges with no cut vertices.
Assuming deletion of one bridge can split its original component into three or more parts.

graph_cut__edge_connectivity.title: Edge cuts and edge connectivity
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.summary: Edge connectivity measures the minimum number of edges that must fail to destroy connectivity.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.definition: For a finite connected undirected graph on at least two vertices, an edge cut is a set of edges whose deletion disconnects the graph. The smallest size is its edge connectivity λ(G). A single bridge is an edge cut of size 1.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.explanation: To prove λ(G)=k, show that k edges suffice and fewer than k cannot disconnect the graph. Deleting all edges incident to a vertex isolates it, so λ(G) is at most minimum degree, though this upper bound need not be attained.
notation: λ(G)=min{|F|:G−F is disconnected}.
A connected graph has a bridge exactly when λ(G)=1.
graph_cut__edge_connectivity.example: Deleting any one triangle edge leaves it connected; deleting the two edges at one vertex disconnects it. Thus λ(K₃)=2.
common_mistakes: Claiming λ=k from one k-edge cut without proving a lower bound.
Confusing edge connectivity, which deletes edges, with vertex connectivity, which deletes vertices.

graph_weighted.title: Weighted graphs
graph_weighted.summary: Weighted graphs attach numbers to edges to represent cost, length, and other quantities; path comparison requires adding edge weights.
graph_weighted.definition: A weighted graph consists of G=(V,E) with a weight function w:E→ℝ. Weights may represent length, time, cost, or another specified quantity. The weight w(P) of a path or walk sums the weights of traversed edges, counting repetitions. State explicitly whether negative weights, directions, or repeated traversal are allowed.
graph_weighted.explanation: A path with the fewest edges need not have minimum total weight. A zero-weight edge is still present and must be distinguished from a missing edge. Cost matrices usually use ∞ for missing edges and 0 for the cost of an empty walk at a vertex. Being weighted implies neither nonnegative weights nor the triangle inequality. With repeated traversal, negative closed walks may make cost unbounded below, so algorithmic assumptions matter.
notation: w(e) is the weight of e; w(P)=Σe along P w(e), counting each traversal.
A missing direct edge is usually ∞ in a cost matrix; an empty-walk diagonal cost is 0.
In an undirected weighted graph, both directions use the same edge and weight.
graph_weighted.example: If st has weight 9 and s—a—b—t has three edges of weight 2, the direct edge uses fewer edges but the three-edge path has lower cost, 6.
common_mistakes: Confusing fewest edges with minimum total weight.
Using 0 for both missing edges and valid zero-weight edges.
Applying any shortest-path algorithm without checking negative weights or directions.

graph_weighted__path_cost.title: Edge weights, path costs, and optimization objectives
graph_weighted__path_cost.summary: Path cost is the sum of edge weights; edge count, cost, and bottleneck objectives differ.
graph_weighted__path_cost.definition: A weight function w:E→ℝ assigns a number to every edge. Total walk cost sums edge weights with multiplicity. A minimum edge-count path is a minimum-cost path when every edge has weight 1.
graph_weighted__path_cost.explanation: Costs may represent time, distance, or price, and different meanings of weights may give different optimal routes on the same graph. If a problem instead minimizes the maximum edge weight as a bottleneck objective, optimize that quantity rather than the sum.
notation: w(P)=Σ along P w(e).
Name edge-count length and weighted cost separately.
graph_weighted__path_cost.example: A route with weights 1 and 8 costs 9; a route with three edges of weight 2 costs 6. The latter has more edges but is cheaper.
common_mistakes: Ignoring weights and counting only steps.
Calling a route best without specifying the objective.

graph_weighted__cost_matrix.title: Cost matrices and zero-weight edges
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.summary: A cost matrix must distinguish actual zero-cost edges from missing direct edges.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.definition: Fix a vertex order. In a cost matrix C, cᵢⱼ is the weight of the direct edge from vᵢ to vⱼ; use ∞ when no direct edge exists and usually 0 on the diagonal for an empty walk. C is symmetric for undirected graphs but generally not for directed graphs.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.explanation: A cost matrix is not an all-pairs shortest-distance matrix: an indirect route must not fill a missing-edge entry. Special structures such as negative loops need separate diagonal conventions; this entry uses loopless models.
notation: cᵢⱼ=∞ means no direct edge, not necessarily that no route through intermediate vertices exists.
For undirected graphs, cᵢⱼ=cⱼᵢ.
graph_weighted__cost_matrix.example: With only a→b of weight 0 and b→c of weight 2, cₐ𝚌=∞ although the minimum total cost from a to c is 2.
common_mistakes: Replacing direct costs by shortest distances without explanation.
Forcing a directed cost matrix to be symmetric.

graph_weighted__negative_walks.title: Negative closed walks and repetition rules
graph_weighted__negative_walks.summary: Whether negative weights cause unbounded cost depends on repeatability and reachability from the source and to the target.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.definition: A closed walk has identical endpoints and is a negative-cost closed walk if its total weight is negative. If the source can reach it and the target remains reachable afterward, repeat it arbitrarily many times to make source-to-target cost unbounded below.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.explanation: One negative directed edge need not create a negative cycle. A directed acyclic graph has only finitely many simple paths even with negative edges. An undirected negative edge can be traversed back and forth to create a negative closed walk, but repetition is forbidden if only simple paths are allowed.
notation: If w(C)<0, k repetitions cost kw(C).
A negative closed walk affects s-to-t cost only if s can reach it and it can reach t.
graph_weighted__negative_walks.example: A directed edge a→b of weight −2, without any route back to a, does not by itself imply all costs are unbounded below.
common_mistakes: Assuming any negative edge guarantees a negative cycle.
Repeating a negative edge in a problem allowing only simple paths.

graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.title: Total cost, edge count, and bottleneck objectives
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.summary: An optimal route must be defined relative to a specific numerical objective.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.definition: The total-cost objective minimizes the sum of edge weights; the fewest-edges objective minimizes edge count; the bottleneck objective minimizes the largest individual edge weight along the path. These are three different optimization problems.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.explanation: The objectives may select different routes. Giving weights does not automatically specify an objective; both model and answer should state the quantity optimized. Fewest edges and minimum total cost naturally agree when all edges have the same positive weight.
notation: Total cost Σw(e); edge count |E(P)|; bottleneck maxe along P w(e).
Routes can be compared as better only under the same objective.
graph_weighted__optimization_objectives.example: Weights 1,8 give total cost 9 and bottleneck 8; weights 4,4,4 give total cost 12 and bottleneck 4. The two objectives prefer opposite routes.
common_mistakes: Assuming more uniform weights mean lower total cost.
Replacing minimum maximum-edge weight with minimum total weight.

graph_euler.title: Eulerian graphs
graph_euler.summary: Euler traversals use each edge exactly once; their key conditions involve connectivity of the nonisolated part and vertex degrees.
graph_euler.definition: An Euler trail traverses every edge exactly once and may repeat vertices. If its endpoints coincide, it is an Euler circuit. A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an Euler circuit exactly when all nonzero-degree vertices lie in one component and all degrees are even. It has an Euler trail with distinct endpoints exactly when the nonzero-degree part is connected and precisely two vertices have odd degree.
graph_euler.explanation: Many textbooks call a connected undirected graph with an Euler circuit Eulerian. When asking only whether all edges can be traversed, isolated vertices can be ignored. Every visit to an internal vertex consumes one entering and one leaving edge, pairing its degree contributions; an open trail’s endpoints are exceptions. Directed graphs must respect arc directions: strong connectivity of the nonzero-degree part and equality of indegree and outdegree at each vertex guarantee an Euler circuit. Euler problems cover edges, rather than requiring each vertex to appear once.
notation: Euler trail: every edge exactly once; Euler circuit: additionally equal endpoints.
An open undirected Euler trail starts and ends at the two odd-degree vertices.
A directed Euler circuit requires d⁺(v)=d⁻(v) at every vertex and the connectivity condition on the nonzero-degree part.
graph_euler.example: Add diagonal ac to a—b—c—d—a. Vertices a,c have degree 3 and the others degree 2. The sequence a—b—c—d—a—c uses all five edges once, giving an Euler trail from a to c, but no Euler circuit exists.
common_mistakes: Remembering each vertex once instead of each edge once.
Checking degree parity without checking that all edges lie in one traversable connected part.
Applying undirected degree criteria to directed graphs while ignoring indegrees, outdegrees, and directions.

graph_euler__undirected_circuit.title: The even-degree criterion for undirected Euler circuits
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.summary: An undirected Euler circuit requires all edges to be continuously accessible and edge ends to pair at each vertex.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.definition: A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an Euler circuit exactly when all nonzero-degree vertices lie in one connected component and all vertex degrees are even. An Euler circuit uses every edge once and returns to its start.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.explanation: Isolated vertices have no edges to traverse and may be ignored in the existence test. Even degrees come from pairing each entry with an exit. Connectivity ensures no edges remain in an unreachable part.
notation: The nonzero-degree part is connected and ∀v, deg(v) is even.
A loop contributes degree 2 and therefore does not disrupt even parity.
graph_euler__undirected_circuit.example: A triangle plus an isolated vertex still has an Euler circuit covering all edges; two disjoint triangles do not.
common_mistakes: Checking only even degrees and overlooking connectivity of the part containing edges.
Rejecting every graph with an isolated vertex as having no closed traversal of all edges.

graph_euler__directed_balance.title: Directed Euler circuits and degree balance
graph_euler__directed_balance.summary: A directed Euler circuit must balance entries and exits at each vertex and access all arcs.
graph_euler__directed_balance.definition: A directed Euler circuit follows directions and uses every arc exactly once. If there is at least one arc, strong connectivity of the nonzero-degree part and d⁺(v)=d⁻(v) at every vertex are sufficient and necessary for its existence.
graph_euler__directed_balance.explanation: Equality of total indegree and total outdegree holds in every directed graph and is far from sufficient. Check each vertex and exclude arcs scattered among parts that cannot all be visited together.
notation: A directed Euler circuit requires ∀v, d⁺(v)=d⁻(v).
A directed Euler trail with distinct endpoints has indegree/outdegree imbalances of 1 at its two endpoints.
graph_euler__directed_balance.example: In a→b→c→a, every indegree and outdegree is 1, giving a directed Euler circuit. Two disjoint directed cycles are balanced at every vertex but cannot form one circuit.
common_mistakes: Using undirected parity in place of directed indegree/outdegree balance.
Checking only total degrees rather than each vertex.

graph_euler__construction.title: Constructing Euler traversals and tracking edge identities
graph_euler__construction.summary: Splicing closed trails or adding and removing an auxiliary edge constructs Euler traversals; parallel edges must be used by their own identities.
graph_euler__construction.definition: In a finite connected undirected graph with even degrees, start anywhere and follow unused edges to form a closed trail. If unused edges remain, start another closed trail at an existing trail vertex incident to an unused edge and splice it in, continuing until all edges are used. Parallel edges are distinct, and each loop is also used once.
graph_euler__construction.explanation: This is construction by splicing closed trails. With two odd-degree vertices, first add an auxiliary edge to make all degrees even, then cut the Euler circuit at that edge. An algorithm should record unique edge identifiers rather than just endpoint pairs.
notation: Distinguish used and unused edges by edge identifiers.
A loop contributes degree 2 but appears only once in an Euler traversal.
graph_euler__construction.example: Two parallel edges e₁,e₂ between a,b give the Euler circuit a—e₁—b—e₂—a; this does not repeat the same edge.
common_mistakes: Merging two parallel edges into one.
Interpreting a loop’s degree contribution of 2 as requiring two traversals.

graph_euler__open_trail.title: Open Euler trails and two odd-degree vertices
graph_euler__open_trail.summary: An all-edge traversal with distinct endpoints requires exactly two odd-degree endpoints.
graph_euler__open_trail.definition: A finite undirected graph with at least one edge has an open Euler trail exactly when the nonzero-degree part is connected and exactly two vertices have odd degree. Those two vertices must be its endpoints; every other vertex has even degree.
graph_euler__open_trail.explanation: Internal entries and exits pair, leaving one unpaired incidence at each endpoint. Add an auxiliary edge between the odd vertices to obtain an even-degree Euler circuit, then cut it open to construct a trail in the original graph.
notation: Exactly two odd-degree vertices, rather than at least two.
Vertices may repeat in the trail, but edges may not.
graph_euler__open_trail.example: Adding a diagonal to a quadrilateral makes the diagonal’s endpoints odd; they can be the endpoints of an open Euler trail.
common_mistakes: Mistaking two odd vertices as a criterion for an Euler circuit.
Choosing an even-degree vertex as an endpoint of an open Euler trail.

q_number_inverse_crt_02.title: Combining three coprime moduli
q_number_inverse_crt_02.statement: Find the least nonnegative solution and all integer solutions of x≡1(mod 4), x≡2(mod 7), x≡3(mod 9).
q_number_inverse_crt_02.answer_text: The least nonnegative solution is 93; all integer solutions are x=93+252k, k∈ℤ.
q_number_inverse_crt_02.explanation: The first two conditions combine to x≡9(mod 28): substitute x=1+4t modulo 7 to get 4t≡1, hence t≡2 and x=9+28s. Substituting modulo 9, with 28≡1(mod 9), gives s≡3(mod 9). Thus x=9+28(3+9k)=93+252k. Since 4,7,9 are pairwise coprime, the solution is unique modulo 252.
q_number_inverse_crt_02.grading_criteria: Correctly combine first modulo 28 and then modulo 9, obtain 93 and period 252, and check all three remainders.

q_number_inverse_crt_03.title: Noncoprime moduli do not always give a product period
q_number_inverse_crt_03.statement: Which form describes all integer solutions of x≡1(mod 4), x≡3(mod 6)?
q_number_inverse_crt_03.explanation: The remainder difference 2 is divisible by gcd(4,6)=2, so solutions exist. Write x=1+4t, giving 4t≡2(mod 6), or 2t≡1(mod 3), hence t≡2(mod 3). Thus x=9+12k, with period lcm(4,6)=12.
q_number_inverse_crt_03.grading_criteria: Choose C; distinguish period 12, the least common multiple, from the product 24.

options.text: Every odd integer is a solution.

q_number_inverse_crt_04.title: Proving existence and uniqueness for two moduli
q_number_inverse_crt_04.statement: Let m,n be coprime positive integers. Prove that for any integers a,b, the system x≡a(mod m), x≡b(mod n) has a solution unique modulo mn.
q_number_inverse_crt_04.answer_text: Take um+vn=1 and set x₀=avn+bum. It satisfies both congruences. The difference of any two solutions is divisible by m and n, hence by mn since they are coprime.
q_number_inverse_crt_04.explanation: Since gcd(m,n)=1, there are integers u,v with um+vn=1. Set x₀=avn+bum. Modulo m, vn≡1 and um≡0, so x₀≡a; modulo n, um≡1 and vn≡0, so x₀≡b. If x,y are solutions, m∣(x−y) and n∣(x−y). Write x−y=mt. From n∣mt and gcd(m,n)=1, n∣t, so mn∣(x−y), proving uniqueness modulo mn.
q_number_inverse_crt_04.grading_criteria: Half credit for the Bézout construction and checking both congruences; half for proving any two solutions differ by a multiple of mn.

q_number_inverse_crt_05.title: Direct construction with CRT weights
q_number_inverse_crt_05.statement: Use inverse weights to find the least nonnegative solution of x≡4(mod5), x≡6(mod7).
q_number_inverse_crt_05.explanation: M=35. For modulus 5, M₁=7 has inverse 3 and weight 21. For modulus 7, M₂=5 also has inverse 3 and weight 15. Thus x≡4·21+6·15=174≡34(mod35). Check that 34 has remainder 4 modulo 5 and 6 modulo 7.
q_number_inverse_crt_05.grading_criteria: Both weights, the linear combination, final reduction, and checks must be correct.

q_number_inverse_crt_06.title: Constructing weights for three moduli
q_number_inverse_crt_06.statement: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to find the least nonnegative solution of x≡1(mod3), x≡2(mod5), x≡3(mod7), and give one set of three CRT weights.
q_number_inverse_crt_06.answer_text: Weights 70,21,15 work; the least nonnegative solution is 52.
q_number_inverse_crt_06.explanation: M=105. M₁=35 has inverse 2 modulo 3, giving weight 70; M₂=21 has inverse 1 modulo 5, giving weight 21; M₃=15 has inverse 1 modulo 7, giving weight 15. The linear combination is 70+2·21+3·15=157≡52(mod105). Each weight is 1 modulo its own modulus and 0 modulo the others.
q_number_inverse_crt_06.grading_criteria: Most credit is for the weights and inverse conditions; reduce 157 modulo 105 and check the remainders.

q_number_inverse_crt_07.title: Incompatibility from a common factor
q_number_inverse_crt_07.statement: Does x≡2(mod6), x≡3(mod9) have an integer solution? Explain.
q_number_inverse_crt_07.answer_text: No solution, since gcd(6,9)=3 does not divide 2−3=−1.
q_number_inverse_crt_07.explanation: The first congruence gives x≡2(mod3), while the second gives x≡0(mod3). One integer cannot lie in two distinct residue classes modulo 3, so there is no solution. Equivalently, the common factor 3 does not divide the remainder difference −1.
q_number_inverse_crt_07.grading_criteria: State that there is no solution and explain either the conflict modulo 3 or failure of the gcd solvability condition.

q_number_inverse_crt_08.title: Common execution days for two periodic tasks
q_number_inverse_crt_08.statement: Number days starting at day 0. Task A runs when t≡1(mod4), and task B when t≡2(mod5). Find the earliest positive common execution day and all common days from 1 through 100.
q_number_inverse_crt_08.explanation: Set t=1+4k. Modulo 5 this gives 4k≡1, hence k≡4(mod5), so t≡17(mod20). All common days are 17+20j; imposing 1≤t≤100 gives five values.
q_number_inverse_crt_08.grading_criteria: Correctly model the congruences, obtain period 20 and earliest positive day 17, and list every value in range.

q_number_linear_congruence_01.title: Check linear-congruence solvability first
q_number_linear_congruence_01.statement: How many residue classes modulo 9 solve 6x≡5(mod 9) over the integers?
q_number_linear_congruence_01.explanation: gcd(6,9)=3, but 3 does not divide 5. Thus there is no integer solution and no solution residue class modulo 9.
q_number_linear_congruence_01.grading_criteria: Choose A; use or explain that the gcd does not divide the right side.

q_number_linear_congruence_02.title: All residue solutions with a noncoprime coefficient
q_number_linear_congruence_02.statement: Solve 6x≡8(mod 14), listing all representatives between 0 and 13.
q_number_linear_congruence_02.explanation: gcd(6,14)=2 divides 8, so there are two solution classes modulo 14. Reduce to 3x≡4(mod 7). Since 3·5≡1(mod 7), x≡20≡6(mod 7). Lifting modulo 14 gives 6 and 13. Check 6·6=36≡8 and 6·13=78≡8(mod 14).
q_number_linear_congruence_02.grading_criteria: Include solvability, reduction, inverse calculation, both solutions, and their checks.

q_number_linear_congruence_03.title: Minimum production batches for packaging
q_number_linear_congruence_03.statement: Each batch produces 12 parts. Packing all parts into boxes of 20 leaves exactly 8 parts. What is the minimum number of batches? The batch count must be a positive integer.
q_number_linear_congruence_03.explanation: Let x be the batch count. Then 12x≡8(mod 20). As gcd(12,20)=4, reduce to 3x≡2(mod 5). The inverse of 3 modulo 5 is 2, so x≡4(mod 5), with minimum positive solution 4. The 48 parts fill 2 boxes and leave 8.
q_number_linear_congruence_03.grading_criteria: Set up the correct congruence, reduce to x≡4(mod 5), choose 4 using positivity, and check.

q_number_linear_congruence_04.title: Solvability and the number of residue classes
q_number_linear_congruence_04.statement: Let m>0 and g=gcd(a,m). Prove ax≡b(mod m) is solvable if and only if g∣b, and explain why there are exactly g solution classes modulo m when it is solvable.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.answer_text: Necessity follows from ax−my=b. If g∣b, a/g and m/g are coprime, giving a unique solution x₀ modulo m/g. The solutions modulo m are exactly x₀+k(m/g), k=0,…,g−1.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.explanation: If a solution exists, ax−my=b for some integer y. Since g divides both terms on the left, g∣b. Conversely, if g∣b, put a′=a/g,b′=b/g,m′=m/g. Since gcd(a′,m′)=1, Bézout gives an inverse of a′ modulo m′, so a′x≡b′(mod m′) has exactly one solution class x₀. All integer solutions are x=x₀+km′. Taking k=0,…,g−1 gives g distinct classes modulo m; other k repeat them.
q_number_linear_congruence_04.grading_criteria: All three parts are required: necessity, coprime reduction with existence and uniqueness, and lifting to exactly g classes.

q_number_linear_congruence_05.title: Which right sides permit a solution?
q_number_linear_congruence_05.statement: For 8x≡b(mod12), which listed values of b make the congruence solvable?
q_number_linear_congruence_05.explanation: gcd(8,12)=4, so solvability is equivalent to 4∣b. Among 1,4,6,8, only 4 and 8 satisfy it.
q_number_linear_congruence_05.grading_criteria: Choose B,D only; the gcd 4 determines the answer.

q_number_linear_congruence_06.title: Finding a modular inverse
q_number_linear_congruence_06.statement: Find the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 26, using a representative from 0 through 25, and check the product.
q_number_linear_congruence_06.grading_criteria: Include a correct extended Euclidean or equivalent calculation, standard representative 15, and product verification.

q_number_linear_congruence_07.title: Solving a congruence with a right side other than 1
q_number_linear_congruence_07.explanation: gcd(5,18)=1, so 5 is invertible. As 5·11=55≡1(mod18), multiplication by 11 gives x≡77≡5(mod18). Every solution lies in this class; check 5·5=25≡7.
q_number_linear_congruence_07.grading_criteria: Find the correct inverse, reduce to 5, and give all integer solutions with period 18.

q_number_linear_congruence_08.title: Combining congruences with a finite range
q_number_linear_congruence_08.statement: Find all integers x satisfying 6x≡9(mod15) and 1≤x≤20.
q_number_linear_congruence_08.explanation: gcd(6,15)=3 divides 9, so reduce to 2x≡3(mod5). The inverse of 2 modulo 5 is 3, giving x≡9≡4(mod5). Between 1 and 20 this progression gives exactly 4,9,14,19.
q_number_linear_congruence_08.grading_criteria: First obtain the complete congruence class, then accurately select the four values in range.

q_number_prime_01.title: Identifying a prime
q_number_prime_01.statement: Which positive integer below is prime?
q_number_prime_01.explanation: 49=7² and 91=7·13, while 1 is not prime by definition. For 53, test only the primes 2,3,5,7 up to √53. None divides 53, so it is prime.
q_number_prime_01.grading_criteria: Choose C; explaining the trial-division bound and rejecting the other choices may support process feedback.

q_number_prime_02.title: Prime factorization and counting positive divisors
q_number_prime_02.statement: Express 756 as a product of prime powers and find its number of positive divisors.
q_number_prime_02.explanation: Repeated division by 2 leaves 189, and 189=3³·7, so 756=2²·3³·7. Every positive divisor has form 2ᵃ3ᵇ7ᶜ with a∈{0,1,2}, b∈{0,1,2,3}, c∈{0,1}. Thus there are 3·4·2=24.
q_number_prime_02.grading_criteria: Half credit for correct prime factorization; half for the choices for each exponent and the result 24.

q_number_prime_03.title: Divisibility is closed under integer linear combinations
q_number_prime_03.statement: Let a,b,c be integers with a≠0, a∣b, and a∣c. Prove a∣(4b−3c).
q_number_prime_03.answer_text: Take integers u,v with b=au,c=av. Then 4b−3c=a(4u−3v), so a∣(4b−3c).
q_number_prime_03.explanation: There are integers u,v with b=au,c=av. Then 4b−3c=4au−3av=a(4u−3v). Since 4u−3v is an integer, the definition of divisibility gives the conclusion.
q_number_prime_03.grading_criteria: Full credit requires integer-multiple representations, correct substitution, and noting that the remaining factor is an integer.

q_number_prime_04.title: Why primes cannot be exhausted by a finite list
q_number_prime_04.statement: Prove there are infinitely many primes. Explain why the integer constructed has a prime factor absent from the assumed finite list.
q_number_prime_04.answer_text: Suppose all primes are p₁,…,pₖ and take N=p₁⋯pₖ+1. Since N>1 it has a prime factor q, but no pᵢ divides N. Thus q is absent from the list, a contradiction.
q_number_prime_04.explanation: Suppose the only primes are p₁,…,pₖ. Set N=p₁⋯pₖ+1>1. Prime factorization gives at least one prime divisor q of N. For every i, N has remainder 1 modulo pᵢ, so pᵢ does not divide N. Thus q is none of the listed primes, contradicting completeness of the list. There is no need, and no justification, to claim N itself must be prime.
q_number_prime_04.grading_criteria: Explain every step: the finite-list assumption, construction of N, existence of a prime factor, exclusion of that factor from the list, and contradiction.

q_number_prime_05.title: Proving transitivity from the divisibility definition
q_number_prime_05.statement: Let a,b,c be nonzero integers with a∣b and b∣c. Prove a∣c.
q_number_prime_05.answer_text: From b=au and c=bv, obtain c=a(uv), where uv is an integer.
q_number_prime_05.explanation: There are integers u,v such that b=au and c=bv. Substitution gives c=(au)v=a(uv). Since uv∈ℤ, the definition gives a∣c.
q_number_prime_05.grading_criteria: Give both integer-multiple representations and complete the substitution; arrows merely repeating the hypotheses are insufficient.

q_number_prime_06.title: Square-root trial division identifies a composite
q_number_prime_06.statement: Determine whether 221 is prime or composite and give a prime factor no greater than √221.
q_number_prime_06.answer_text: 221 is composite; 13≤√221 is a prime factor, and 221=13·17.
q_number_prime_06.explanation: 14²=196<221<225=15², so √221 lies between 14 and 15. Testing 2,3,5,7,11,13 finds that 13 divides 221 with quotient 17. Thus 221 is composite and 13 is in the required trial range.
q_number_prime_06.grading_criteria: Correct classification, a nontrivial factorization, and verification of the square-root bound are all required.

q_number_prime_07.title: Counting perfect-square divisors
q_number_prime_07.statement: Given 756=2²·3³·7, find all its positive perfect-square divisors.
q_number_prime_07.explanation: Every prime exponent in a perfect square must be even. The exponent of 2 can be 0 or 2, that of 3 can be 0 or 2, and that of 7 must be 0. The four choices give 1,2²=4,3²=9,2²·3²=36, with no others.
q_number_prime_07.grading_criteria: State that exponents must be even and list all four divisors without repetition or omission.

q_number_prime_08.title: Refuting an assertion that always produces primes
q_number_prime_08.statement: After checking several small nonnegative integers n, someone claims n²+n+41 is prime for every nonnegative integer n. Give a specific counterexample and explain why finitely many successful checks cannot prove the assertion.
q_number_prime_08.answer_text: Take n=40: 40²+40+41=1681=41² is composite. Finite checks do not cover all nonnegative integers.
q_number_prime_08.explanation: For n=40, the expression is 1600+40+41=1681=41·41, which has nontrivial factor 41 and disproves the universal assertion. Calculations at small n verify only those cases and cannot rule out composite values at unchecked n.
q_number_prime_08.grading_criteria: Give a valid n, correct arithmetic and composite factorization, and explain that a universal conclusion requires a general proof.

q_number_rsa_01.title: Choosing a public exponent for toy RSA
q_number_rsa_01.statement: For classroom demonstration only, toy RSA uses p=5,q=11. Which e satisfies the public-exponent requirement gcd(e,φ(n))=1? These parameters must not be used for real encryption.
q_number_rsa_01.explanation: n=55 and φ(n)=4·10=40. The gcds with 40 are 2 for e=2, 5 for e=5, 1 for e=7, and 10 for e=10. Thus only e=7 satisfies the condition.
q_number_rsa_01.grading_criteria: Choose C and check against φ(n)=40, not n=55.

q_number_rsa_02.title: One encryption and decryption with toy RSA
q_number_rsa_02.statement: Toy RSA uses p=5,q=11,e=3 and message m=7. Find the private exponent d with 0<d<40, the ciphertext c, and verify decryption. This is only a modular-arithmetic lesson, not secure encryption parameters.
q_number_rsa_02.explanation: φ(55)=40. From 3d≡1(mod 40), d=27 since 3·27=81. The ciphertext is 7³=343≡13(mod 55). Square-and-multiply gives 13²≡4,13⁴≡16,13⁸≡36,13¹⁶≡31(mod 55). Since 27=16+8+2+1, 13²⁷≡31·36·4·13≡7(mod 55), recovering the message.
q_number_rsa_02.grading_criteria: One third each for inverse d, encryption c, and modular-power verification of decryption; results must be in the appropriate modulus ranges.

q_number_rsa_03.title: Toy RSA when the message is not coprime
q_number_rsa_03.statement: Toy RSA uses p=3,q=11,n=33,e=3,d=7 and message m=3, which is not coprime to n. Compute encryption and decryption, and explain why Euler’s theorem modulo 33 cannot be applied directly to m. This is for teaching only.
q_number_rsa_03.answer_text: c=27 and 27⁷≡3(mod 33). Euler’s theorem cannot be used directly since gcd(3,33)=3.
q_number_rsa_03.explanation: The ciphertext is 3³=27. Since 27²≡3 and 27⁴≡9(mod 33), 27⁷≡9·3·27=729≡3(mod 33). Recovery still works for this noncoprime message. For a proof, both sides are 0 modulo 3; use Fermat’s little theorem modulo 11 and then CRT. Euler’s theorem a^φ(n)≡1 requires gcd(a,n)=1, which fails here.
q_number_rsa_03.grading_criteria: Include the ciphertext, square-and-multiply decryption, the failed coprimality condition, and an explanation using CRT.

q_number_rsa_04.title: Correctness of classroom RSA for all messages
q_number_rsa_04.statement: Let p,q be distinct primes, n=pq, and e,d positive integers with ed≡1(mod (p−1)(q−1)). Prove m^(ed)≡m(mod n) for every integer m, including messages not coprime to n. This concerns algebraic correctness of a teaching algorithm and is not a security argument for a real system.
q_number_rsa_04.answer_text: Work modulo p and q separately, distinguishing whether each divides m. In the nondivisible cases, ed−1 is a multiple of the prime minus 1, so apply Fermat’s little theorem. CRT then gives the result modulo pq.
q_number_rsa_04.explanation: Write ed=1+k(p−1)(q−1) for a nonnegative integer k. Modulo p, if p∣m then both m^(ed) and m are 0. Otherwise Fermat gives m^(p−1)≡1, so m^(ed)=m·(m^(p−1))^(k(q−1))≡m. Similarly modulo q, both sides are 0 if q∣m, and otherwise use m^(q−1)≡1. Since p,q are coprime, divisibility of m^(ed)−m by both implies divisibility by pq.
q_number_rsa_04.grading_criteria: For each prime modulus cover both divisibility cases, then combine by coprimality or CRT; citing Euler’s theorem modulo n alone is insufficient.

q_number_rsa_05.title: Another set of classroom key parameters
q_number_rsa_05.statement: Toy RSA uses distinct primes p=7,q=11 and public exponent e=7. Find n,φ(n), and the private exponent with 0<d<60. This is a classroom example and must not be used for real encryption.
q_number_rsa_05.grading_criteria: Give the modulus, Euler totient, and correct modular inverse.

q_number_rsa_06.title: A message divisible by a prime factor in classroom RSA
q_number_rsa_06.statement: Toy RSA uses n=55,e=3,d=27,m=5. Compute the ciphertext and check modulo 5 and modulo 11 that decryption recovers 5. This illustrates the teaching algorithm only, without addressing real security.
q_number_rsa_06.answer_text: The ciphertext is 15 and the decrypted residue is 5.
q_number_rsa_06.explanation: 5³=125≡15(mod55). Modulo 5, 15²⁷≡0, matching 5. Modulo 11, 15≡4 and 4¹⁰≡1, so 4²⁷≡4⁷. Since 4²≡5 and 4⁴≡3, 4⁷≡3·5·4=60≡5. The unique solution modulo 55 with residue 0 modulo 5 and 5 modulo 11 is 5, so decryption recovers 5.
q_number_rsa_06.grading_criteria: Correctly give ciphertext 15, checks modulo 5 and 11, and CRT combination to 5.

q_number_rsa_07.title: Algebraic demonstrations versus real encryption security
q_number_rsa_07.statement: Which statement correctly describes a classroom textbook-RSA example using small primes and no randomized padding?
q_number_rsa_07.explanation: The example verifies algebraic relations involving modular powers, inverses, and CRT, but small parameters are easily factored. The deterministic unpadded process also lacks the full security properties required in real systems. Classroom correctness calculations therefore cannot directly serve as a secure encryption scheme.
q_number_rsa_07.grading_criteria: Choose B; distinguish correctness, meaning recovery of messages, from security, meaning resistance to attacks.

options.text: Successful recovery on decryption proves suitability for real encryption.
It illustrates algebraic correctness but cannot directly be used as real secure encryption.
Small primes guarantee security as long as the private exponent is not written down.
Existence of a modular inverse itself makes factorization absolutely impossible.

q_number_rsa_08.title: Determinism of the classroom unpadded procedure
q_number_rsa_08.statement: Using the same toy public key n=55,e=3, will two direct calculations of mᵉ modn for integer message m=7 give the same ciphertext? Compute it and explain why this does not guarantee real cryptographic security.
q_number_rsa_08.answer_text: Both give 13. Direct textbook modular exponentiation is deterministic; correct decryption does not imply real encryption security.
q_number_rsa_08.explanation: For fixed m,e,n, exponentiation and remainder give a unique result: 7³=343≡13(mod55), so both ciphertexts are equal. There is no random step. This illustrates a teaching transform; invertibility alone does not establish resistance to attacks. Real systems additionally require standard encoding, randomization, and secure implementation; these toy parameters cannot be used directly.
q_number_rsa_08.grading_criteria: Include ciphertext 13 both times, the reason for determinism, and the distinction between correctness and real security.

q_count_basic_01.title: Mutually exclusive resource choices
q_count_basic_01.statement: A shelf has 4 distinct popular-science booklets and 3 distinct history booklets, with no overlap between the categories. How many ways are there to borrow exactly 1?
q_count_basic_01.explanation: Borrowing science and borrowing history are disjoint exhaustive alternatives. The sum rule gives 4+3=7; the task does not ask for one of each.
q_count_basic_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for B; 0 for any other choice.

q_count_basic_02.title: A passcode with nonrepeating digits
q_count_basic_02.statement: A passcode consists of 1 letter followed by 2 digits. Choose the letter from A,B,C and digits from 0,1,2,3,4. The two digits must differ, and the digit part may start with 0. Count the passcodes.
q_count_basic_02.explanation: There are 3 letter choices, 5 first-digit choices, and exactly 4 second-digit choices after excluding the chosen first digit. Each triple uniquely determines a code, so the product rule gives 3×5×4=60. Do not exclude leading 0 or identify different digit orders.
q_count_basic_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 3 letters and 5 first digits, 4 for the 4 second digits and order, and 3 for 60.

q_count_basic_03.title: Conditions for counting principles
q_count_basic_03.statement: Let A,B be arbitrary finite sets. Which assertions always hold?
q_count_basic_03.explanation: The Cartesian product consists of ordered pairs, so A is correct even if A and B intersect. B ignores overlap. C describes a true partition, disjoint and exhaustive, permitting the sum rule. D is false: positions of successive choices are usually part of the result, so exchanging order need not give the same object.
q_count_basic_03.grading_criteria: 10 points for exactly A,C; 5 for omissions without wrong selections; 0 if any incorrect option is selected.

options.text: If objects are divided into pairwise disjoint exhaustive classes, their class sizes can be added.
The order of results from two steps can always be ignored.

q_count_basic_04.title: Pairing even- and odd-parity binary strings
q_count_basic_04.statement: Let n≥1 be an integer. Prove that exactly $2^{n-1}$ binary strings of length n have an even number of ones. Explain why the correspondence used omits and repeats nothing.
q_count_basic_04.answer_text: Flipping the first bit bijects strings with even and odd numbers of ones; each class has $2^{n-1}$ elements.
q_count_basic_04.explanation: Partition the 2^n length-n strings into E and O by even or odd number of ones. They are disjoint and exhaustive. Define f by flipping the first bit and keeping all other bits. This adds or removes one 1, so f maps E to O. Flipping again restores the original string, giving an inverse and hence a bijection. Thus |E|=|O|; the sum rule gives 2|E|=2^n, so |E|=2^(n−1). The assumption n≥1 ensures a first bit exists.
q_count_basic_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the partition and total, 3 for the flip and parity change, 3 for invertibility, and 2 for the count and n≥1.

q_count_perm_comb_01.title: A review group without roles
q_count_perm_comb_01.statement: How many groups of 3 can be selected from 7 distinct volunteers if no roles are assigned?
q_count_perm_comb_01.explanation: The member set alone determines the group, without internal order. Compute C(7,3)=7×6×5/(3×2×1)=35. The count 7×6×5=210 counts the 6 orderings of each group separately.
q_count_perm_comb_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for A; 0 for other choices.

q_count_perm_comb_02.title: Both member categories must be represented
q_count_perm_comb_02.statement: A project has 5 engineers and 4 designers, all distinct. Select a group of 3 with no roles, including at least 1 person from each category. Count the groups.
q_count_perm_comb_02.explanation: Classify by engineer count: 1 engineer and 2 designers gives C(5,1)C(4,2)=5×6=30 groups; 2 engineers and 1 designer gives C(5,2)C(4,1)=10×4=40. These disjoint cases exhaust the valid groups, giving 30+40=70. With no roles, do not multiply by 3!.
q_count_perm_comb_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for complete case division, 3 for each combination product, and 2 for total 70.

q_count_perm_comb_03.title: Distinct arrangements of repeated labels
q_count_perm_comb_03.statement: Six labels read A,A,B,B,B,C. Equal letters are indistinguishable. How many distinct strings result from arranging them in a row?
q_count_perm_comb_03.explanation: Temporarily number equal labels. The 6 distinct labels have 6! arrangements. Removing numbers, every string has exactly 2!3! representations from the permutations of the two As and three Bs. Thus there are 720/(2×6)=60 strings. The denominator’s 1! for the single C can be omitted.
q_count_perm_comb_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for 6! labeled arrangements, 5 for explaining multiplicity 2!3!, and 3 for division and result 60.

q_count_perm_comb_04.title: A group-with-convener identity
q_count_perm_comb_04.statement: For 1≤k≤n, prove $k\binom nk=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ by counting. Specify the common objects counted by both sides.
q_count_perm_comb_04.answer_text: Both sides count selecting k of n people and designating one selected person as convener.
q_count_perm_comb_04.explanation: Let the people form an n-element set. Count pairs (S,c), where S is a k-element subset and c∈S. Choosing S first and c within S gives C(n,k)k. Choosing c from all n people first, then k−1 of the remaining n−1 to join S, gives nC(n−1,k−1). Both constructions biject to the same objects, so the counts agree. The range 1≤k≤n makes the choices meaningful.
q_count_perm_comb_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for specifying common objects, 3 for group then person, 3 for person then other members, and 1 for the conclusion and range.

q_count_binomial_01.title: Extracting a coefficient in a simple expansion
q_count_binomial_01.explanation: Producing x² requires exactly 2 of the 5 factors to contribute x and the others 1, so the coefficient is C(5,2)=10.
q_count_binomial_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for 10; identifying C(5,2) suffices, without a full expansion.

q_count_binomial_02.title: A specified term with a negative constant
q_count_binomial_02.explanation: Choose 4 of the 6 factors to contribute 2x and the remaining 2 to contribute −3. The coefficient is C(6,4)·2⁴·(−3)²=15×16×9=2160. The negative sign occurs an even number of times, giving a positive result.
q_count_binomial_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the combination count, 4 for the two power factors and sign, and 3 for 2160.

q_count_binomial_03.title: Sums of binomial coefficients
q_count_binomial_03.statement: Let n be a positive integer. Which identities hold for every such n?
q_count_binomial_03.explanation: A follows from (1+1)^n. B follows from (1−1)^n=0 for n≥1. For C, sum kC(n,k)=nC(n−1,k−1) over k to get n·2^(n−1), or differentiate (1+x)^n and set x=1. D fails at n=2: the left side is 1+4+1=6 but the right side is 4. The correct square sum is C(2n,n).
q_count_binomial_03.grading_criteria: 10 points for exactly A,B,C; 5 for omissions without wrong selections; 0 if any incorrect option is selected.

q_count_binomial_04.title: A two-group selection proof of the square sum
q_count_binomial_04.statement: For a nonnegative integer n, prove $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}{n}$. Give a complete combinatorial or coefficient-comparison argument.
q_count_binomial_04.answer_text: Choose n elements from the union of two disjoint n-element sets and classify by the number k chosen from the first.
q_count_binomial_04.explanation: Let A,B be disjoint sets of size n. Directly choosing an n-element subset of A∪B gives C(2n,n). Classify by the number k chosen from A; then n−k come from B, giving C(n,k)C(n,n−k)=C(n,k)². The cases k=0,…,n are disjoint and exhaustive, so their sum equals the total. For n=0, both sides equal 1, representing the unique empty selection.
q_count_binomial_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the objects chosen from 2n elements, 3 for complete classification by k, 3 for each product and symmetry, and 2 for summation and the n=0 boundary.

q_count_pigeonhole_01.title: A guaranteed lower bound on label repetitions
q_count_pigeonhole_01.statement: Each of 15 cards has one of 7 labels. Regardless of the assignment, some label must occur at least how many times? Find the largest guaranteed integer.
q_count_pigeonhole_01.explanation: Divide cards into 7 label classes. If every class had at most 2 cards, there would be at most 14, so some class has at least 3. The distribution 3,2,2,2,2,2,2 has 15 cards and no class of size 4, so the largest guarantee is exactly 3.
q_count_pigeonhole_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for B; 0 for other choices.

q_count_pigeonhole_02.title: Divisibility of a difference of measurements
q_count_pigeonhole_02.statement: Eight devices each produce an integer measurement, possibly equal or negative. Prove that two distinct devices have measurements whose difference is divisible by 7.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.answer_text: Classify the devices by the 7 remainders modulo 7; two of the 8 must share a class.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.explanation: Every integer has a unique remainder 0,1,…,6 modulo 7; negative integers use the same congruence classes. Place the 8 devices in 7 boxes by measurement remainder. Two distinct devices must share a box, with measurements u,v satisfying u−v=7t for some integer t. Equal measurements give difference 0, also divisible by 7, so repetitions cause no problem.
q_count_pigeonhole_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 7 residue classes, 3 for assigning 8 devices and applying the principle, and 4 for divisibility and handling repeated or negative values.

q_count_pigeonhole_03.title: A guaranteed sum from complementary pairs
q_count_pigeonhole_03.statement: Choose any 13 distinct integers from {1,2,…,24}. Prove that two sum to 25, and explain why choosing 12 need not suffice.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.answer_text: Use pairs {1,24},{2,23},…,{12,13}. Thirteen numbers fill some pair. The set {1,…,12} shows 12 do not guarantee it.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.explanation: Partition the 24 integers into 12 disjoint boxes {i,25−i}, 1≤i≤12. Each box contains two numbers summing to 25. With 13 distinct selected numbers, some box contains both of its numbers, giving the pair. Choosing only 1 through 12 gives no pair summing to 25, so 13 is the minimum guaranteed quantity.
q_count_pigeonhole_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for a complete 12-pair partition, 4 for distinctness and the pigeonhole argument, and 2 for a 12-number counterexample.

q_count_pigeonhole_04.title: Integer points and an integer midpoint
q_count_pigeonhole_04.statement: Five distinct points in the plane have integer coordinates. Prove that two have a segment midpoint whose two coordinates are also integers.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.answer_text: Classify points into 4 coordinate-parity types. Two of the same type have even sums in each coordinate.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.explanation: There are four coordinate-parity types: (even,even),(even,odd),(odd,even),(odd,odd). Of 5 distinct points, two distinct points P=(x1,y1),Q=(x2,y2) share a type. Thus x1+x2 and y1+y2 are both even, making ((x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2) integral. Each coordinate must have matching parity across the points; the horizontal and vertical coordinates of one point need not match each other.
q_count_pigeonhole_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for the 4 types, 3 for finding distinct points of one type, and 4 for proving both midpoint coordinates integral.

q_count_inclusion_01.title: Overlap of two conditions
q_count_inclusion_01.statement: Among some records, 12 have label A, 9 have label B, and 4 have both. How many have at least one label?
q_count_inclusion_01.explanation: Adding gives 21, counting the 4 double-labeled records twice. Subtract their intersection once: 12+9−4=17.
q_count_inclusion_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for C; 0 for other choices.

q_count_inclusion_02.title: Accounting for three properties
q_count_inclusion_02.statement: Among 100 devices, 40 have A,35 have B,30 have C; 12 have A and B,10 have A and C,9 have B and C, and 4 have all three. Pairwise counts include devices with all three. Find the numbers with at least one property, exactly one, and none.
q_count_inclusion_02.answer_text: At least one:78; exactly one:55; none:22.
q_count_inclusion_02.explanation: The union has 40+35+30−12−10−9+4=78 devices, so 100−78=22 have none. Only A: 40−12−10+4=22; only B:35−12−9+4=18; only C:30−10−9+4=15. Exactly one totals 22+18+15=55. As a check, exactly two is (12−4)+(10−4)+(9−4)=19, and 55+19+4=78.
q_count_inclusion_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for union 78 and its formula, 5 for the individual only counts 22,18,15 and total 55, and 2 for complement 22.

q_count_inclusion_03.title: Surjective assignment to three locations
q_count_inclusion_03.statement: Assign 5 distinct exhibits to 3 exhibition areas labeled A,B,C, each exhibit in exactly one area and every area nonempty. Count the assignments and explain the need for intersection corrections.
q_count_inclusion_03.explanation: There are 3⁵=243 unrestricted assignments. Let A_A denote that area A is empty, with analogous events for the others. A specified empty area leaves 2⁵ assignments, totaling 3·2⁵. If two specified areas are empty, all exhibits go to the remaining one, giving 1 assignment for each of C(3,2)=3 pairs. All three cannot be empty because there are 5 exhibits. Inclusion–exclusion gives 243−96+3=150. Subtracting only 3·2⁵ removes assignments using one area twice, so intersections must be added back.
q_count_inclusion_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for universe 3⁵, 3 for empty-area events and 3·2⁵, 3 for pairwise and triple intersections, and 2 for 150.

q_count_inclusion_04.title: An inclusion–exclusion proof of misplaced letters
q_count_inclusion_04.statement: Four letters and four envelopes are each numbered 1 through 4, with one letter per envelope. Prove that exactly 9 assignments put no letter in its matching envelope. Explain every inclusion–exclusion term.
q_count_inclusion_04.explanation: All assignments are bijections between distinct letters and envelopes, totaling 4!. Let A_i mean letter i enters its matching envelope. Fixing k correct letters fixes their destinations, leaving (4−k)! arrangements of the rest. The k letters can be chosen in C(4,k) ways. Thus the count with no correct letter is Σ(k=0 to 4)(−1)^k C(4,k)(4−k)!=24−24+12−4+1=9. The last term 1 is the all-correct assignment, with 0!=1.
q_count_inclusion_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for the universe and bad events, 4 for intersections (4−k)! and choices C(4,k), 2 for alternating summation, and 2 for result 9 and the final term.

q_count_generating_01.title: Formal encoding of a geometric sequence
q_count_generating_01.statement: Let $a_n=2^n$ (n≥0). As a formal power series, its ordinary generating function $A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ is ____.
q_count_generating_01.explanation: The formal expansion 1/(1−2x)=1+2x+4x²+8x³+… has coefficient 2^n at x^n. Multiplying this series by 1−2x gives constant coefficient 1 and cancellation at every other degree, so it is the formal inverse of 1−2x.
q_count_generating_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for 1/(1−2x); no numerical convergence condition is needed.

q_count_generating_02.title: Coefficients for two package sizes
q_count_generating_02.statement: A product comes in packages of 2 units and 3 units. Any nonnegative number of each may be used; packages of the same size are indistinguishable and selection order is ignored. How many ways give exactly 12 units? Give the generating function and coefficient.
q_count_generating_02.answer_text: The generating function is $1/((1-x^2)(1-x^3))$, and the required coefficient is 3.
q_count_generating_02.explanation: Choosing 0,1,2,… two-unit packages gives 1+x²+x⁴+…=1/(1−x²), and three-unit packages give 1/(1−x³). The x¹² coefficient of their product counts nonnegative solutions of 2u+3v=12. Parity makes v even, and 0≤v≤4, so v=0,2,4 with u=6,3,0 respectively: 3 ways. Indistinguishability and ignored order mean no extra permutation factor.
q_count_generating_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 2 for each factor, 2 for 2u+3v=12, and 4 for all three solutions and count 3.

q_count_generating_03.title: Initial terms in recurrence shifts
q_count_generating_03.statement: The sequence satisfies $a_0=1$ and $a_n=a_{n-1}+n$ (n≥1). Use formal power series to find A(x) and an expression for a_n. You may use $\sum_{n\ge1}nx^n=x/(1-x)^2$.
q_count_generating_03.explanation: Multiply by x^n and sum over n≥1. The left side is A(x)−1, the lagged-term sum is xA(x), and the final sum is x/(1−x)². Hence (1−x)A(x)=1+x/(1−x)², giving A(x)=1/(1−x)+x/(1−x)³=(1−x+x²)/(1−x)³. Iterating the recurrence also gives a_n=1+1+2+…+n=1+n(n+1)/2, including n=0.
q_count_generating_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for shifts A−1 and xA, 3 for the generating function, and 3 for the general term and n=0 check.

q_count_generating_04.title: Do formal identities require convergence after substitution?
q_count_generating_04.statement: Someone says: “$\sum_{n\ge0}x^n=1/(1-x)$ cannot be a generating-function identity because the left side diverges at x=2.” Explain the flaw and verify the identity using formal multiplication.
q_count_generating_04.answer_text: Formal series identities compare coefficients and do not require summation at x=2; (1−x)(1+x+x²+…)=1 holds coefficientwise.
q_count_generating_04.explanation: In formal power series, x is a symbol; substituting any number to form an infinite numerical sum is not automatic. Set S=Σ(n≥0)x^n. The constant coefficient of (1−x)S is 1, while every x^n coefficient for n≥1 is 1−1=0. Thus the product is 1. Since 1−x has constant coefficient 1, it has a unique formal inverse, giving S=1/(1−x). Under a separate analytic interpretation the geometric series converges only for |x|<1; divergence at x=2 does not invalidate the formal identity.
q_count_generating_04.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for formal versus analytic interpretation, 4 for coefficientwise multiplication, 2 for inverse reasoning or equivalent, and 1 for analytic condition |x|<1.

q_recurrence_model_01.title: Boundary values for a strip-tiling recurrence
q_recurrence_model_01.statement: Let a_n count tilings of a length-n strip using indistinguishable tiles of lengths 1 and 2, with one empty tiling. Which recurrence and initial values are correct?
q_recurrence_model_01.explanation: For n≥2, a first tile of length 1 corresponds to any tiling of length n−1, and a first tile of length 2 to any tiling of length n−2. The cases are disjoint and exhaustive. Since a_0=1 and a_1=1, A is correct; a_0 cannot be 0.
q_recurrence_model_01.grading_criteria: 10 points for A; 0 for other choices.

q_recurrence_model_02.title: Codes with no adjacent ones
q_recurrence_model_02.statement: Let b_n count binary strings of length n with no adjacent ones, including one empty string. Give a recurrence with sufficient initial conditions and find b_6.
q_recurrence_model_02.explanation: For n≥2, classify by ending. Removing a final 0 leaves any valid length-(n−1) string, giving b_(n−1). A final 1 must be preceded by 0; removing the final 01 leaves any valid length-(n−2) string, giving b_(n−2), with unique reconstruction. The disjoint cases add. b_0=1 and b_1=2 (0,1), giving b_2=3,b_3=5,b_4=8,b_5=13,b_6=21.
q_recurrence_model_02.grading_criteria: 10 points: 4 for the ending cases and reversible correspondences, 3 for range and two initial values, and 3 for 21.

q_recurrence_model_03.title: Divide-and-conquer at odd sizes
q_recurrence_model_03.statement: An algorithm costs 1 unit for 1 element. For n≥2, it splits into subproblems of sizes ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉, processes both, then spends n additional units. Let T_n be total cost. Give its recurrence and find T_5.
q_recurrence_model_03.explanation: Both subproblems execute, so add their costs rather than taking a maximum or product, and include the extra n. For odd n the subproblem sizes differ and cannot both be n/2. T_2=1+1+2=4, T_3=T_1+T_2+3=8, and T_5=T_2+T_3+5=4+8+5=17. No T_0 is needed, since both subproblem sizes are at least 1 for n≥2.
q_recurrence_model_03.grading_criteria: 10 points: 3 for integer subproblem sizes, 3 for summing both costs, adding n, and the base value, and 4 for T_2,T_3,T_5=17.

q_recurrence_model_04.title: Stairs with no consecutive two-step moves
